title: What held up
hook: sleep, exercise, social ties and practice effects have strong support

segments.voice: Yesterday: the replication crisis, a hundred studies run again and only about a third holding clearly. Your line was was it repeated. Did anyone quote a study at you? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

So, after yesterday, is anything left standing? It's a fair question, and the wrong conclusion is easy to reach: if some famous findings shrank or vanished, maybe none of it means anything. Go to bed whenever. Skip the walk. Cancel the dinner. That isn't what the record shows. Some findings have been tested not once but over and over, by different teams, in different countries, with different methods, and pooled together in large reviews. They don't make headlines anymore, because they're old news. Today is about the old news. The boring findings that held up.
screen: `IS ANYTHING LEFT STANDING?` → `TESTED OVER AND OVER.` → `THE BORING FINDINGS.`

segments.voice: First, sleep. A review that pooled studies of lost sleep found a clear pattern: short on sleep, people think, remember and manage their moods worse. A Psalm in the King James text says it gently: "for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Sleep there is a gift, not a reward for finishing everything. Second, moving your body. Exercise has been tested against low mood in many trials, and reviews of them find it helps, though how much varies from study to study. Third, other people. A large review led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad pooled studies on social relationships and found that people with stronger ties tended to live longer. Ecclesiastes saw the shape of it: "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." Fourth, practice itself, modestly. A large review of meditation programs, led by Madhav Goyal, found moderate evidence that they eased anxiety, depression and pain a little. Not a cure, and not shown to beat other active treatments, like exercise. But it held up. Notice what these four share. None is new. None is a trick. Each one has been checked by the neighbor many times and is still standing. That's what held up means: not one bright study, but many ordinary ones agreeing.
screen: `SLEEP HELD UP.` · `MOVING YOUR BODY HELD UP.` · `OTHER PEOPLE HELD UP.` · `PRACTICE HELD UP, MODESTLY.` · then, large: `MANY ORDINARY STUDIES AGREEING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose from the sturdy shelf. Settle, and let the breath slow. Let the four come up one at a time: sleep, movement, people, practice. Notice which one your life is shortest on right now. Don't judge it. Just notice. Then picture the smallest real version of it for tonight or tomorrow. Lights out a little earlier. A walk around the block. A message to one friend. These two minutes, again tomorrow. Let that one picture settle and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
What held up. Sleep, movement, social ties and practice: findings tested over and over that are still standing. Today's word.
Your line: what held up. Today, do the small version you pictured, and let a boring finding do its quiet work. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Health researchers trust findings that many independent studies agree on, gathered in reviews that pool them; sleep, physical activity and social connection are among the findings with this kind of support.

fork.setup: after hearing that many famous findings shrank when repeated, what do you do?
options: decide none of it means anything.
lean on the findings that were tested over and over.
only trust the newest, most surprising studies.
fork.reveal: the record doesn't say nothing works. it says to trust what many studies agree on: sleep, movement, people, and modestly, practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: after the replication crisis, nothing in psychology can be trusted.
what it means: some findings have been tested over and over and still stand: sleep, movement, social ties, practice.
what a scholar hears: pooled reviews of many studies, like Holt-Lunstad's on social ties and Goyal's on meditation, are what 'held up' looks like.

sources.ref: Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton, "Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review" (PLoS Medicine)
Goyal et al., "Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being" (JAMA Internal Medicine)
Pilcher and Huffcutt, "Effects of sleep deprivation on performance: a meta-analysis" (Sleep)
Cochrane review, "Exercise for depression" (Cooney et al.)

notes: Confirm the summaries: Pilcher and Huffcutt pooled sleep-deprivation studies showing worse cognitive performance and mood; the voice says 'think, remember and manage their moods worse'.

Confirm the exercise summary against the Cochrane review (Cooney et al.): exercise moderately reduces depressive symptoms versus control; effect sizes vary and shrink in higher-quality trials. The voice says 'helps, though how much varies'.
Confirm Holt-Lunstad et al.: stronger social relationships associated with greater likelihood of survival. No percentages given.

Confirm Goyal et al.: moderate evidence of small improvements in anxiety, depression and pain; no evidence meditation programs were better than active treatments (drugs, exercise, other behavioral therapies).
Editor pass: 'reviews ... find the same thing again and again' about sleep became 'a review that pooled studies ... found a clear pattern', matching the one cited meta-analysis.
'Different countries, different methods' in the hook is a general description of the evidence base; check it reads fairly.
Psalm 127:2 and Ecclesiastes 4:10 are used as lines with the same shape, not as evidence.
